claim: Parhyale hawaiensis can regenerate their limbs independently of the site of amputation.
source: Parhyale can regenerate their limbs independently of the site of amputation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is supported by citations to previous work (Alwes et al., 2016; Konstantinides and Averof, 2014).

claim: Regeneration occurs in the distal part of the limb stump, within the exoskeleton of the amputated leg.
source: Regeneration occurs in the distal part of the limb stump, within the exoskeleton of the amputated leg (Figures 1 and 2; Alwes et al., 2016; Konstantinides and Averof, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to figures in the manuscript and citations to previous studies.

claim: By amputating the T4 or T5 legs of mid-sized adults at the distal part of the carpus, the entire regenerating tissue can be captured within a single field of view using a 20× objective.
source: We have found that by amputating the T4 or T5 legs of mid-sized adults at the distal part of the carpus, we can capture the entire regenerating tissue within a single field of view using a 20× objective (Zeiss Plan-Apochromat 20×/0.8) (see Figure 2, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a methodological finding supported by data shown in figures and videos.

claim: Within 24 hours post amputation, a melanised scab forms at the site of injury.
source: Within 24 hours post amputation (hpa), a melanised scab forms at the site of injury (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Epithelial cells stretch and migrate to cover the wounded surface under the scab between 10-30 hours post amputation.
source: This is accompanied by stretching and migration of epithelial cells to cover the wounded surface, under the scab (10–30 hpa in Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is observed in the live imaging videos.

claim: There is little (if any) cell division during the early stages of regeneration (first 24-30 hours).
source: There is little (if any) cell division during these early stages (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Between 1 and 3.5 days post amputation, the epithelium detaches from the scab.
source: Between 1 and 3.5 days post amputation, the epithelium detaches from the scab (Figure 2C; 31 hpa in Video 1, 65 hpa in Video 2).
evidence: This is observed in the live imaging data shown in figures and videos.

claim: Epithelial detachment often coincides with the onset of cell proliferation, cell-cell rearrangements and apoptosis in cells within ~100 µm from the scab.
source: The timing of detachment varies considerably (Figure 3), but we find that it often coincides with the onset of cell proliferation, cell–cell rearrangements and apoptosis in the cells that lie within ~100 µm from the scab.
evidence: This correlation is observed in the data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: More proximally located tissues detach from the cuticle and retract towards the body, making space for the growth of regenerating tissues in the distal part of the stump.
source: More proximally located tissues detach from the cuticle and retract towards the body, making space for the growth of regenerating tissues in the distal part of the stump (40–85 hpa in Video 1; 80–120 hpa in Video 2).
evidence: This is observed in the live imaging videos.

claim: The boundaries of the leg podomeres typically appear within a day from epithelial detachment.
source: The boundaries of the leg podomeres typically appear within a day from epithelial detachment (Figure 2D, E; 45–60 hpa in Video 1; 80–95 hpa in Video 2).
evidence: This timing is observed in the live imaging data.

claim: In some recordings, the tissues making up the podomeres can be seen pulsating with a periodicity of 6-7 hours.
source: In some recordings, the tissues making up the podomeres can be seen pulsating with a periodicity of 6–7 h (see 105–145 hpa in Video 2).
evidence: This observation is made from the live imaging data shown in Video 2.

claim: The rates of cell proliferation and movement gradually decline and nuclear positions within the tissue become stabilised in later stages of regeneration.
source: Later, the rates of cell proliferation and movement gradually decline and the nuclear positions within the tissue become stabilised (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is observed in the live imaging data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Many cells differentiate during the late phase of regeneration when nuclear positions become stabilised.
source: Based on transcriptome profiling data, we think that many cells differentiate during this phase (Sinigaglia et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from transcriptome profiling data cited from a previous study.

claim: Once regeneration is completed, the newly regenerated leg is trapped inside the exoskeleton of the amputated leg stump.
source: Once regeneration is completed, the newly regenerated leg is trapped inside the exoskeleton of the amputated leg stump.
evidence: This is a direct observation stated in the text.

claim: The regenerated leg is released from the old exoskeleton and becomes functional during the animal's next molt.
source: It is released from the old exoskeleton and becomes functional during the animal's next molt.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the regeneration process.

claim: When the animal molts, the regenerated leg is fully formed.
source: When the animal molts, the regenerated leg is fully formed (Almazán et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The timing of regeneration events varies from leg to leg, but their order is consistent in all recordings.
source: The timing of these events varies from leg to leg, but their order is consistent in all our recordings (summarised in Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of observations across multiple recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fastest recordings show the leg of a young adult regenerating in less than 3 days at 29°C.
source: Our fastest recordings show the leg of a young adult regenerating in less than 3 days at 29°C (li51-t4 and li51-t5).
evidence: This is a specific observation from the experimental data.

claim: The longest regeneration recordings take ~10 days to complete regeneration at 26-27°C.
source: In contrast, the longest ones take ~10 days to complete regeneration (li16-t5 and li34-t4, imaged at 26–27°C).
evidence: This is a specific observation from the experimental data.

claim: The overall speed of leg regeneration is determined largely by variation in the speed of the early (wound closure) phase of regeneration.
source: We find that the overall speed of leg regeneration is determined largely by variation in the speed of the early (wound closure) phase of regeneration, and to a lesser extent by variation in later phases when leg morphogenesis takes place (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from analysis of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no clear relationship between the relative duration of each phase and the speed of regeneration.
source: There is no clear relationship between the relative duration of each phase and the speed of regeneration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 A',B').
evidence: This is concluded from analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pairs of adjacent T4 and T5 legs that were amputated simultaneously appear to regenerate at a similar pace.
source: We note that pairs of adjacent T4 and T5 legs that were amputated simultaneously (in datasets li24, li41, li48, li51, and li5) appear to regenerate at a similar pace, suggesting variation in the speed of regeneration is influenced by systemic factors, such as the age, health or physiology of the individual.
evidence: This observation is made from the data and leads to an inference about systemic factors.

claim: Some cells undergo apoptosis during the course of regeneration.
source: During the course of regeneration, some cells undergo apoptosis (reported in Alwes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Using the H2B-mRFPruby marker, apoptotic cells appear as bright pyknotic nuclei that break up and become engulfed by circulating phagocytes.
source: Using the H2B-mRFPruby marker, apoptotic cells appear as bright pyknotic nuclei that break up and become engulfed by circulating phagocytes (see bright specks in Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Apoptosis can be observed in regenerating legs that have not been subjected to live imaging.
source: While some cell death might be caused by photodamage, apoptosis can also be observed in regenerating legs that have not been subjected to live imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most cells in the upper slices of image stacks (top 30 μm) can be tracked with a high degree of confidence using semi-automated cell tracking.
source: Using this mode of semi-automated cell tracking, we find that most cells in the upper slices of our image stacks (top 30 μm) can be tracked with a high degree of confidence.
evidence: This is a finding from the cell tracking analysis.

claim: A smaller proportion of cells is trackable in deeper layers of the image stacks.
source: A smaller proportion of cells is trackable in deeper layers (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Improving the z resolution should be the preferred option when taking into account the efforts required for proofreading.
source: We conclude that improving the z resolution (condition #2) should be the preferred option when taking into account the efforts required for proofreading.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis presented in Table 1A.

claim: Improving both z and t resolution will be valuable for tracking more rapid changes or when users seek the best tracking performance from Elephant without proofreading.
source: Improving both z and t resolution (condition #4 or #5) will be valuable for tracking more rapid changes, or when users seek the best tracking performance from Elephant, without proofreading (e.g. automated tracking).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis in Table 1A.

claim: Under the settings tested, deconvolution and denoising did not help to improve cell tracking performance.
source: We find that, under the settings tested, deconvolution and denoising did not help to improve cell tracking performance (Table 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Table 1B.

claim: Regenerating legs can be fixed and immunofluorescently stained after long-term live imaging.
source: We showed that regenerating legs could be fixed and immunofluorescently stained after long-term live imaging.
evidence: This is a methodological achievement demonstrated in the study.

claim: Stained cells can be identified in the live recordings and tracked.
source: The stained cells could then be identified in the live recordings and tracked (Figure 6A, A').
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A, A'.

claim: Using single-nucleus transcriptional profiling, approximately 15 transcriptionally distinct cell types were previously identified in adult Parhyale legs.
source: Using single-nucleus transcriptional profiling, we previously identified approximately 15 transcriptionally distinct cell types in adult Parhyale legs (Almazán et al., 2022), including epidermis, muscle, neurons, haemocytes, and a number of still unidentified cell types.
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The chitinous exoskeleton surrounding adult legs is impermeable to probes or gives high unspecific staining in conventional in situ hybridisation.
source: Numerous efforts to apply in situ hybridisation protocols on Parhyale legs have failed in the past, because the chitinous exoskeleton surrounding the adult legs is impermeable to probes or gives high unspecific staining.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge from previous attempts.

claim: The permeability problem was partly solved for antibodies by fragmenting the legs and using long incubation times.
source: By fragmenting the legs and using long incubation times, the permeability problem was partly solved for antibodies (Almazán et al., 2022) but could not be overcome with conventional in situ hybridisation probes, presumably due to their large molecular size.
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hybridisation chain reaction (HCR) is a sensitive in situ hybridisation method that makes use of much shorter probes.
source: We therefore turned to hybridisation chain reaction (HCR), a sensitive in situ hybridisation method that makes use of much shorter probes (Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claim: The adapted HCR method allows labeling of specific populations of cells, such as neurons and mechanosensory organs, in late embryos and adult legs.
source: Using this method, we are able to label specific populations of cells, such as neurons (using probes for futsch, Hummel et al., 2000) and mechanosensory organs (using probes for nompA, Chung et al., 2001), in late embryos and adult legs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: This is the first time an in situ hybridisation approach has been successfully applied in adult legs, overcoming the cuticular permeability barrier.
source: This is the first time we are able to apply an in situ hybridisation approach in adult legs, overcoming the cuticular permeability barrier.
evidence: This is stated as a novel achievement of the study.

claim: HCR can be applied to regenerated legs immediately after live imaging to locate stained cells in the live image recordings.
source: As described earlier for immunostainings, we applied HCR to regenerated legs immediately after live imaging and were able to locate the stained cells in the live image recordings.
evidence: This is a methodological achievement demonstrated in the study.

claim: This approach allows tracking the origins of molecularly identified cells during the course of regeneration.
source: This approach allows us to track the origins of molecularly identified cells during the course of regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a capability enabled by the method.

claim: In Drosophila, spineless is expressed in a ring of cells in the distal part of developing legs.
source: In Drosophila, spineless is expressed in a ring of cells in the distal part of developing legs; it encodes a transcription factor that plays a role in patterning of the tarsal segments (Duncan et al., 1998; Natori et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work on Drosophila.

claim: The spineless orthologue of Parhyale is expressed in a similar pattern at the distal end of the regenerated carpus.
source: We find that the spineless orthologue of Parhyale is expressed in a similar pattern at the distal end of the regenerated carpus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell tracking reveals that the spineless-expressing cells of the distal carpus originate from epidermal cells that were widely dispersed in the carpus at the time of amputation.
source: Cell tracking reveals that the spineless-expressing cells of the distal carpus originate from epidermal cells that were widely dispersed in the carpus at the time of amputation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: These epidermal progenitors undergo 0, 1, or 2 cell divisions and generate mostly spineless-expressing cells.
source: These epidermal progenitors undergo 0, 1, or 2 cell divisions and generate mostly spineless-expressing cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parhyale stands out as an experimental system in which the entire process of leg regeneration can be imaged at single-cell resolution.
source: Parhyale stands out as an experimental system in which we can image the entire process of leg regeneration at single-cell resolution and follow the lineages and the fates of cells as the leg is re-made.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the capabilities of the system.

claim: This system provides unique opportunities to identify the progenitors of regenerated tissues, their degree of commitment, locations, division patterns and behaviours during regeneration.
source: This provides unique opportunities to identify the progenitors of regenerated tissues, their degree of commitment, locations, division patterns and behaviours during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the method.

claim: Combined with high-resolution live imaging of developing embryonic legs, this system offers the chance to compare the cellular dynamics of leg regeneration with those of leg development.
source: Combined with high-resolution live imaging of developing embryonic legs (Wolff et al., 2018), it also offers the chance to compare the cellular dynamics of leg regeneration with those of leg development.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Image quality limits the efficiency with which cells can be tracked, particularly in the deeper tissue layers.
source: First, image quality limits the efficiency with which we can track cells, particularly in the deeper tissue layers.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation of the method.

claim: Improved image quality could be achieved with higher numerical aperture objectives, stronger fluorescence signals and longer exposure times.
source: Improved image quality could be achieved with higher numerical aperture objectives, stronger fluorescence signals and longer exposure times, to increase signal-to-noise ratios and resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a potential way to improve the method.

claim: These improvements come with trade-offs in terms of increased light exposure and tissue damage.
source: These improvements, however, come with trade-offs in terms of increased light exposure and tissue damage.
evidence: This is stated as a known constraint.

claim: Light-sheet microscopy would be preferable for minimising light exposure.
source: An obvious improvement, in this respect, would come from replacing confocal microscopy by a more gentle imaging method, such as light-sheet microscopy (Stelzer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a potential improvement, supported by a citation.

claim: The current method for immobilising Parhyale legs for live imaging is incompatible with conventional light-sheet microscopy.
source: Unfortunately, our current method for immobilising Parhyale legs for live imaging is incompatible with conventional light-sheet microscopy, because it requires glueing and imaging the specimens through a glass coverslip.
evidence: This is stated as a technical constraint.

claim: The method described provides the most robust approach to image leg regeneration in Parhyale at present.
source: At present, the method we describe here provides the most robust approach to image leg regeneration in Parhyale.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the current state of the method.

claim: There is a dearth of fluorescent markers that can be used to identify different cell types and cellular transitions during live imaging.
source: A second limitation is the dearth of fluorescent markers that we can use to identify different cell types and cellular transitions during the course of live imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation.

claim: Until fluorescent markers are developed, the in situ labelling approaches described will provide an efficient way to identify different cell fates at the end of live imaging.
source: Until we develop such markers, the in situ labelling approaches described here will provide an efficient way to identify different cell fates at the end of live imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a current solution to the limitation.

claim: Approximately 85% of animals survive the mounting and imaging procedure.
source: Under these conditions, approximately 85% of animals (18 out of 21) survive the mounting and imaging procedure.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments.

claim: Among the imaged legs, approximately 20% show tissue damage/retraction or become arrested before the onset of regeneration.
source: Among the imaged legs, approximately 20% show tissue damage/retraction (5 out of 37) or become arrested before the onset of regeneration (2 out of 37), while 80% go on to regenerate normally.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments.

claim: 80% of imaged legs go on to regenerate normally.
source: Among the imaged legs, approximately 20% show tissue damage/retraction (5 out of 37) or become arrested before the onset of regeneration (2 out of 37), while 80% go on to regenerate normally.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiments.

claim: Live imaging of regeneration presents unique challenges due to the nature of the specimens (large mobile animals), the duration of the process (spanning days or weeks), and the need to achieve cellular resolution without photodamage.
source: High-resolution live imaging of regeneration presents unique challenges due to the nature of the specimens (large mobile animals), the duration of the process (spanning days or weeks), and the fact that cellular resolution must be achieved without damage caused by lengthy exposures to light.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general challenge.

claim: The method includes mounting and long-term live imaging of regenerating legs under conditions that yield high spatial and temporal resolution but minimise photodamage.
source: Our method includes (1) mounting and long-term live imaging of regenerating legs under conditions that yield high spatial and temporal resolution but minimise photodamage
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as part of the method.

claim: The method includes fixing and in situ staining of the regenerated legs that were imaged, to identify cell fates.
source: (2) fixing and in situ staining of the regenerated legs that were imaged, to identify cell fates
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as part of the method.

claim: The method includes computer-assisted cell tracking to determine the cell lineages and progenitors of identified cells.
source: (3) computer-assisted cell tracking to determine the cell lineages and progenitors of identified cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as part of the method.

claim: The method is optimised to limit light exposure while maximising tracking efficiency.
source: The method is optimised to limit light exposure while maximising tracking efficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key feature of the method.

claim: Combined with appropriate cell-type-specific markers, this method may allow the description of cell lineages for every regenerated cell type in the limb.
source: Combined with appropriate cell-type-specific markers, this method may allow the description of cell lineages for every regenerated cell type in the limb.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a potential application.

claim: Unlike developing embryos which can be easily immobilised, regenerating juvenile or adult animals are mobile and cannot easily be fixed under a microscope over long periods of time.
source: First, unlike developing embryos which can be easily immobilised, regenerating juvenile or adult animals are mobile and cannot easily be fixed under a microscope over long periods of time.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the introduction.

claim: Regenerating animals need to move to capture food and, in many cases, to breathe.
source: These animals need to move to capture food and, in many cases, to breathe.
evidence: This is stated as a biological constraint.

claim: Anaesthesia is possible for short periods, but lethal if applied over many hours or days.
source: Anaesthesia is possible for short periods, but lethal if applied over many hours or days.
evidence: This is stated as a constraint on the use of anaesthesia.

claim: Imaging embryonic development has been particularly successful in animals with rapid development.
source: Second, imaging embryonic development has been particularly successful in animals with rapid development.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about developmental imaging.

claim: Developmental processes with a duration of hours or a few days can be followed with high temporal resolution.
source: Developmental processes with a duration of hours or a few days, such as the embryonic development of C. elegans, Drosophila, and zebrafish, or the process of somitogenesis in mice (Keller et al., 2008; Masamizu et al., 2006; Sulston et al., 1983; Tomer et al., 2012), can be followed with high temporal resolution.
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Processes with a longer duration present greater challenges due to the damaging effects that prolonged exposure to light has on living tissues.
source: Processes with a longer duration, however, present greater challenges due to the damaging effects that prolonged exposure to light has on living tissues (Icha et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Long-term live imaging requires robust microscope-camera setups that can maintain image quality and record images over long periods.
source: Long-term live imaging also requires robust microscope-camera setups that can maintain image quality and record images over long periods.
evidence: This is stated as a technical requirement.

claim: Regeneration typically takes place on a timescale of several days or weeks.
source: Regeneration typically takes place on a timescale of several days or weeks.
evidence: This is stated as a general characteristic of regeneration.

claim: The larger size of juvenile or adult organisms can impact live imaging by constraining how large specimens can be mounted on a microscope.
source: Third, the larger size of juvenile or adult organisms can impact live imaging in a number of ways, for example, by constraining how large specimens can be mounted on a microscope (or, indeed, how a microscope might be mounted on the animal, see Aharoni et al., 2019), or by exceeding a microscope's field of view or imaging depth.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge, with a citation to an example.

claim: Live imaging of regeneration under anaesthesia has been developed in zebrafish and mice.
source: In spite of these difficulties, live imaging of regeneration – under anaesthesia – has been developed in zebrafish and mice, allowing for successful imaging of cell dynamics during repair or regeneration in different organs (Chioccioli et al., 2024; Cox et al., 2018; Gurevich et al., 2016; Kamimoto et al., 2020; Mateus et al., 2012; Park et al., 2017; Pineda et al., 2015; Rompolas et al., 2012; Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The duration of continuous time-lapse recordings under anaesthesia has been constrained by poor survival and is typically limited to less than one day.
source: The duration of continuous time-lapse recordings, in these cases, has been constrained by poor survival under long-term anaesthesia and is typically limited to less than one day.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of anaesthesia-based approaches.

claim: An alternative approach has been to immobilise a regenerating animal for the time required to acquire an image stack and then to release it, until the next imaging time point.
source: An alternative approach has been to immobilise a regenerating animal for the time required to acquire an image stack and then to release it, until the next imaging time point when one re-captures the animal and re-visits the same body part.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative approach.

claim: This alternative approach has allowed imaging experiments to run over much longer time periods (several days, even weeks), but with much lower temporal resolution, typically 12 or 24 h between successive time points.
source: This approach has allowed imaging experiments to run over much longer time periods (several days, even weeks), but with much lower temporal resolution, typically 12 or 24 h between successive time points (Chen et al., 2016; Chioccioli et al., 2024; Cox et al., 2018; Currie et al., 2016; De Simone et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2012; Pineda et al., 2015; Rompolas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: A major challenge in the intermittent imaging approach is identifying the same cells at different time points, especially after cell divisions and movements.
source: A major challenge in the latter approach is identifying the same cells at different time points, especially after cell divisions and movements.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge of the approach.

claim: Identifying the same cells can be made easier by sparse labelling of cells, or mosaic labelling of cell clones, for example using Brainbow-like methods.
source: This can be made easier by sparse labelling of cells, or mosaic labelling of cell clones, for example using Brainbow-like methods (Barbosa et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Currie et al., 2016; Ritsma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In recent years, the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis has emerged as a promising experimental system for studying regeneration.
source: In recent years, the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis has emerged as a promising experimental system for studying regeneration, in which transgenic tools can be combined with live imaging (Alwes et al., 2016; Grillo et al., 2016; Konstantinides and Averof, 2014; Paris et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A major advantage of Parhyale for live imaging is the ability to immobilise its regenerating legs over long periods without needing to keep the animals under anaesthesia.
source: For live imaging, a major advantage of Parhyale is our ability to immobilise its regenerating legs over long periods without needing to keep the animals under anaesthesia.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of the system.

claim: Immobilisation is achieved by fixing the chitinous exoskeleton that surrounds the leg onto the microscope coverslip using surgical glue.
source: This is achieved by fixing the chitinous exoskeleton that surrounds the leg onto the microscope coverslip using surgical glue (Alwes et al., 2016; Konstantinides and Averof, 2014).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Parhyale's cuticle is both sturdy and transparent.
source: Thus, Parhyale's cuticle – which is both sturdy and transparent – serves as a straitjacket to immobilise the leg, and as a window through which we can visualise regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the cuticle.

claim: Parhyale's cuticle serves as a straitjacket to immobilise the leg, and as a window through which regeneration can be visualised.
source: Thus, Parhyale's cuticle – which is both sturdy and transparent – serves as a straitjacket to immobilise the leg, and as a window through which we can visualise regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a functional property of the cuticle.

claim: A previous systematic study presented continuous live imaging over periods of 2-3 days, capturing key events of leg regeneration at single-cell resolution.
source: Our first systematic study using this approach presented continuous live imaging over periods of 2–3 days, capturing key events of leg regeneration such as wound closure, cell proliferation and morphogenesis of regenerating legs at single-cell resolution (Alwes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This work extends previous work by developing a method for imaging the entire course of leg regeneration, optimised to reduce photodamage and to improve cell tracking.
source: Here, we extend this work by developing a method for imaging the entire course of leg regeneration, optimised to reduce photodamage and to improve cell tracking.
evidence: This is stated as the goal of the current work.

claim: A method of in situ staining of gene expression in cuticularised adult legs has been developed, which can be combined with live imaging to determine the fate of tracked cells.
source: We also develop a method of in situ staining of gene expression in cuticularised adult legs, which we combine with live imaging to determine the fate of tracked cells.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological development of the current work.

claim: The objective is to image legs during the entire time course of leg regeneration, with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution to support the tracking of individual cells in 3D.
source: Our objective is to image legs during the entire time course of leg regeneration, with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution to support the tracking of individual cells in 3D.
evidence: This is stated as an objective of the work.

claim: The objective includes determining the identities and molecular signatures of the tracked cells.
source: We also want to determine the identities and molecular signatures of the tracked cells.
evidence: This is stated as an objective of the work.

claim: In the long term, this will enable identification of progenitors for each cell type in the leg, tracing their complete genealogies, and characterising the molecular and cell state transitions associated with leg regeneration.
source: In the long term, this will enable us to identify progenitors for each cell type in the leg, to trace their complete genealogies, and to characterise the molecular and cell state transitions associated with leg regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a long-term goal.

claim: Leg regeneration takes place over approximately 1 week in adult Parhyale (3-10 days, depending on the age of the individual, the injury sustained, and other unknown factors).
source: Leg regeneration takes place over approximately 1 week in adult Parhyale (3–10 days, depending on the age of the individual, the injury sustained, and other unknown factors) (Alwes et al., 2016; Konstantinides and Averof, 2014; Sinigaglia et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies showed that imaging at 20-min intervals is sufficient to capture cell divisions and to track cells reliably over time.
source: Our previous studies showed that imaging at 20-min intervals is sufficient to capture cell divisions and to track cells reliably over time (Alwes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A complete recording of a regenerating leg would require capturing at least 360 image stacks, at 20-min intervals, over a period of 5 days.
source: Thus, a complete recording of a regenerating leg would require capturing at least 360 image stacks, at 20-min intervals, over a period of 5 days.
evidence: This is calculated based on the stated requirements.

claim: A major challenge in long-term imaging experiments is balancing the need for high spatial and temporal resolution with the need to minimise photodamage.
source: A major challenge we must address in such long-term imaging experiments is balancing the need for high spatial and temporal resolution with the need to minimise photodamage.
evidence: This is stated as a key challenge.

claim: Increasing spatial or temporal resolution improves the ability to resolve and to track cells in a crowded cellular environment, but also leads to increased light exposure and resulting tissue damage.
source: Increasing spatial or temporal resolution (e.g. by using higher numerical aperture objectives, finer sampling in x, y or z, or shorter imaging intervals) improves our ability to resolve and to track cells in a crowded cellular environment, but also leads to increased light exposure and resulting tissue damage.
evidence: This is stated as a trade-off in imaging.

claim: Confocal microscopy has been used for imaging in this study.
source: Among the various imaging modalities available for live imaging (Schroeder, 2008), we have used confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as the imaging modality used.

claim: Confocal microscopy is now widely established and commercial systems are stable enough to support automated 3D image acquisition over very long time courses.
source: Confocal microscopy is now widely established and commercial systems are stable enough to support automated 3D image acquisition over very long time courses.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for using confocal microscopy.

claim: Live imaging is performed on transgenic animals expressing a histone-bound fluorescent protein expressed under a heat-shock promoter.
source: Live imaging is performed on transgenic animals expressing a histone-bound fluorescent protein expressed under a heat-shock promoter (Alwes et al., 2016; Pavlopoulos et al., 2009; Wolff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claim: To minimise photodamage, imaging is performed at long wavelengths, using a construct expressing H2B-mRFPruby.
source: To minimise photodamage, we image at long wavelengths, using a construct expressing H2B-mRFPruby (Wolff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a strategy to minimise photodamage, supported by a citation.

claim: A heat shock (45 min at 37°C) is applied, typically 12-18 h before amputation, yielding high levels of nuclear fluorescence which can persist for many days in non-dividing cells.
source: To induce transgene expression, a heat shock (45 min at 37°C) is applied, typically 12–18 h before amputation, yielding high levels of nuclear fluorescence which can persist for many days in non-dividing cells.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Heat shocks may be repeated during the course of imaging, using the microscope's temperature-controlled stage, to maintain adequate levels of fluorescence in dividing cells.
source: Heat shocks may be repeated during the course of imaging, using the microscope's temperature-controlled stage, to maintain adequate levels of fluorescence in dividing cells.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: The temperature change during heat shock causes a slight displacement in the acquired images, which is corrected post acquisition.
source: The temperature change causes a slight displacement in the acquired images, which is corrected post acquisition (see Methods).
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail.

claim: Transgenic individuals that show the highest levels of nuclear fluorescence are selected for imaging.
source: To minimise light-induced damage, we select transgenic individuals that show the highest levels of nuclear fluorescence and set the power of the excitation laser to the lowest setting that yields acceptable image quality on our most sensitive GaAsP detector.
evidence: This is stated as a strategy to minimise light-induced damage.

claim: A scanning speed of 2.06 μs per pixel with an averaging of two images (or 1.03 μs per pixel with an averaging of four images) are the fastest settings that generate images of sufficient quality for tracking.
source: To improve image quality while keeping light exposure in check, we have tested different settings for scanning speed and image averaging and determined that a scanning speed of 2.06 μs per pixel with an averaging of two images (or 1.03 μs per pixel with an averaging of four images) are the fastest settings that generate images of sufficient quality for tracking (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from testing different settings, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most animals imaged under these settings regenerate their legs within 5-10 days from amputation.
source: Most animals imaged under these settings regenerate their legs within 5–10 days from amputation (Figure 3), unless they have been amputated shortly before molting.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, shown in Figure 3.

claim: If animals are amputated shortly before molting, the wound is closed and the animals molt before regenerating.
source: In the latter case, the wound is closed and the animals molt before regenerating.
evidence: This is stated as an exception to the typical regeneration timeline.

claim: The regenerating legs of Parhyale make challenging datasets for cell tracking, due to large variations in signal intensity and poor image quality in the deeper tissue layers.
source: The regenerating legs of Parhyale make challenging datasets for cell tracking, due to large variations in signal intensity and poor image quality in the deeper tissue layers.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge for cell tracking.

claim: The challenge is exacerbated by the need to limit the tissues' exposure to light, which constrains signal intensity, spatial and temporal resolution.
source: This is exacerbated by the need to limit the tissues' exposure to light, which constrains signal intensity, spatial and temporal resolution (see above).
evidence: This is stated as an additional challenge.

claim: The datasets capturing the entire course of regeneration are large, typically consisting of image stacks of 15-30 z slices collected over 300-700 time points (i.e. ~10,000 images per dataset).
source: Moreover, the datasets capturing the entire course of regeneration are large, typically consisting of image stacks of 15–30 z slices collected over 300–700 time points (i.e. ~10,000 images per dataset), which makes both manual tracking and proofreading of computer-generated tracks very laborious.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the datasets.

claim: The large size of the datasets makes both manual tracking and proofreading of computer-generated tracks very laborious.
source: Moreover, the datasets capturing the entire course of regeneration are large, typically consisting of image stacks of 15–30 z slices collected over 300–700 time points (i.e. ~10,000 images per dataset), which makes both manual tracking and proofreading of computer-generated tracks very laborious.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the large dataset size.

claim: The initial implementation of Elephant generated tracking predictions over the entire image stack.
source: The initial implementation of Elephant generated tracking predictions over the entire image stack.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the initial implementation.

claim: A 'backtracking' function has been added to Elephant, which allows users to focus on tracking cells of particular interest.
source: We have now added a 'backtracking' function (see Methods), which allows users to focus on tracking cells of particular interest.
evidence: This is stated as a new feature added to Elephant.

claim: With the backtracking function, users are able to select individual cells and obtain predictions on their progenitors, moving up towards earlier points in their cell lineage.
source: With this function, users are able to select individual cells and obtain predictions on their progenitors, moving up towards earlier points in their cell lineage.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the backtracking function.

claim: The backtracking function is particularly useful when specific cells of interest can be identified based on molecular or other markers.
source: This is particularly useful when specific cells of interest can be identified based on molecular or other markers (see below).
evidence: This is stated as an application of the backtracking function.

claim: The detection of nuclei can be enhanced by doubling the z resolution at the expense of xy resolution and image quality.
source: Our results, summarised in Table 1A, show that the detection of nuclei can be enhanced by doubling the z resolution at the expense of xy resolution and image quality (compare detection metrics in #1 versus #2, #4, and #5).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Table 1A.

claim: The improvement in detection by doubling z resolution is particularly evident in the deeper layers of the imaging stacks.
source: This improvement is particularly evident in the deeper layers of the imaging stacks, which are usually the most challenging to track (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tracking of nuclei across time points (linking) can be enhanced by doubling the temporal resolution at the expense of xy resolution and image quality.
source: Tracking of nuclei across time points (linking) can be enhanced by doubling the temporal resolution at the expense of xy resolution and image quality (compare linking metrics in #1 versus #3, #4, and #5).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Table 1A.

claim: The best tracking performance is achieved by improving both z and t resolution, at the expense of xy resolution or image quality.
source: Taking both detection and linking into account, it appears that the best tracking performance is achieved by improving both z and t resolution, at the expense of xy resolution or image quality (conditions #4 and #5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis in Table 1A.

claim: Doubling the temporal resolution requires much more effort for proofreading because the datasets contain many more time points.
source: However, doubling the temporal resolution requires much more effort for proofreading (see last column in Table 1A), because the datasets contain many more time points.
evidence: This is stated as a trade-off, with reference to Table 1A.
